active_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.optimize.minimize with trust-constr method for robust constraint handling
active_paradigms.description: Replace SLSQP with trust-constr method which uses an interior-point algorithm that handles nonlinear inequality constraints more robustly. Trust-constr builds a local quadratic model of the objective and trust region, making it less prone to getting stuck in poor local optima. Keep the Delaunay-based constraint reduction but use trust-constr's superior constraint handling. Increase maxiter to 10000 and use tighter tolerances. Run multiple restarts with different seeds and initial configurations to find better solutions. The interior-point method can navigate complex constraint boundaries more effectively than SLSQP's sequential quadratic programming approach.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Escape local optima that SLSQP gets stuck in, achieve higher sum of radii
active_paradigms.cautions: Trust-constr requires careful constraint formulation; ensure all constraint functions return proper shapes. May be slower per iteration but can find better solutions. Use Jacobian options if possible for efficiency.

active_paradigms.idea: Sequential greedy circle placement with scipy.spatial.distance.cdist for spatial reasoning
active_paradigms.description: Instead of simultaneous optimization, place circles sequentially from largest to smallest. Start by placing the first circle at the center with maximum possible radius. For each subsequent circle, use cdist to compute distances from candidate positions to all existing circle centers, then place the new circle at the position maximizing its radius while respecting all constraints. After placing all 26 circles, apply local optimization to fine-tune positions and radii. This greedy approach with spatial indexing can discover configurations that global optimization misses. Use a grid of candidate positions and select the best one for each new circle based on available space.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Discover novel configurations through sequential construction rather than optimization of fixed topology
active_paradigms.cautions: Greedy placement order matters significantly; try multiple orderings. Must validate final configuration. Local refinement is essential after greedy placement to improve solution quality.

active_paradigms.idea: Voronoi-based radius expansion with scipy.spatial.Voronoi for geometric optimization
active_paradigms.description: Use Voronoi diagrams to identify the geometric space available to each circle. Start with a reasonable initial configuration, then iteratively: (1) compute Voronoi diagram of current centers, (2) for each circle, compute the distance to its Voronoi cell boundaries (both edges and container boundaries), (3) set radius to the minimum distance to any boundary, (4) apply local perturbation to centers to increase total sum of radii, (5) repeat until convergence. This leverages the geometric structure of the packing problem directly. Voronoi cells naturally identify which constraints are active for each circle, enabling efficient radius adjustment without checking all pairs.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Maximize radii based on actual available geometric space using Voronoi cell boundaries
active_paradigms.cautions: Voronoi diagrams can have issues with collinear points; add small perturbations if needed. Must handle Voronoi points outside the unit square. Convergence may require careful step-size control.

tried_paradigms.idea: Penalty-based unconstrained optimization with scipy.optimize.minimize using L-BFGS-B
tried_paradigms.description: Reformulate the constrained optimization problem as an unconstrained problem using quadratic penalty functions for all constraints (boundary and pairwise distance). Instead of using SLSQP with explicit constraints, use scipy.optimize.minimize with L-BFGS-B method which is a gradient-based optimizer that handles unconstrained problems more efficiently. Define the objective as negative sum of radii plus penalty terms that grow quadratically when constraints are violated. Use multiple random initializations and tune the penalty weights to balance constraint satisfaction with objective maximization. This approach is different from the failed interior penalty reformulation because it uses a different optimizer (L-BFGS-B vs SLSQP) and a different penalty formulation.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Primary evaluator score (sum_radii/target) by using a more efficient gradient-based optimizer with penalty reformulation
tried_paradigms.cautions: Tune penalty weights carefully - too weak leads to constraint violations, too strong makes optimization difficult; L-BFGS-B requires smooth objective functions so use smooth penalty terms; ensure gradients are well-behaved near constraint boundaries

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.spatial.Voronoi for geometric radius refinement
tried_paradigms.description: Instead of joint optimization, use Voronoi diagrams to geometrically determine optimal radii. Start with a good center configuration, compute the Voronoi diagram using scipy.spatial.Voronoi, then for each circle set its radius to the minimum distance to its Voronoi cell boundaries (edges or container walls). Iterate this process: adjust centers slightly toward Voronoi cell centers, recompute Voronoi, update radii. This geometric approach directly computes the maximum feasible radius for each circle given the current configuration, avoiding expensive constraint-based optimization.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: sum_radii by leveraging geometric structure of circle packing
tried_paradigms.cautions: Handle Voronoi infinite regions carefully (use bounding box clipping), ensure numerical stability when computing distances to cell boundaries, limit iterations to avoid timeout

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.spatial.distance for sequential greedy placement with ordering
tried_paradigms.description: Place circles sequentially using a smart ordering strategy rather than joint optimization. First, determine circle ordering based on a hexagonal lattice pattern (corners first, then edges, then interior). For each circle in order, use scipy.spatial.distance.cdist to compute distances to all previously placed circles, then place it at the position that maximizes its radius while respecting all constraints. Use a fine grid search or analytical solution to find the optimal position for each circle given the constraints from already-placed circles. This sequential approach avoids the curse of dimensionality in joint optimization.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: sum_radii by placing larger circles in optimal positions first
tried_paradigms.cautions: Ordering strategy is critical - corners and edges should be prioritized, use sufficiently fine position search grid, ensure all 26 circles fit within constraints

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.spatial.Delaunay for neighbor-constrained local optimization
tried_paradigms.description: Use Delaunay triangulation to identify which circles are actually constraining each other, then optimize only those critical pairs. Build a Delaunay triangulation of circle centers using scipy.spatial.Delaunay, extract the neighbor graph, and for each circle only consider constraints from its Delaunay neighbors (typically 6 in hexagonal packing). This reduces the number of active constraints from 325 to approximately 156, making optimization more efficient. Then use a simpler local optimization that only enforces these neighbor constraints, allowing faster convergence to better solutions.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: sum_radii by focusing optimization on critical constraint pairs
tried_paradigms.cautions: Ensure Delaunay triangulation handles boundary circles correctly, some non-neighbor pairs may still need checking for validity, maintain full validation at the end

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.spatial.distance.cdist for complete pairwise constraint formulation
tried_paradigms.description: Instead of relying on Delaunay triangulation to identify neighbors (which may miss critical constraints), compute all pairwise distances using scipy.spatial.distance.cdist upfront. This creates a complete constraint matrix where every circle pair that could potentially overlap is explicitly constrained. The key insight is that Delaunay triangulation only captures local neighbors, but in dense packings, non-Delaunay pairs can become critical as circles expand. After computing the full distance matrix, identify pairs where the current distance is within 2.5x the sum of radii as 'critical pairs' and constrain only those, reducing from O(n²) to O(kn) constraints while ensuring no critical constraints are missed. This provides a more complete constraint set than the current Delaunay approach.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Primary sum_radii metric by ensuring all critical circle pairs are properly constrained, preventing local optima from incomplete constraint formulation
tried_paradigms.cautions: Must dynamically update critical pair identification during optimization iterations, use efficient distance computation to avoid O(n²) overhead at each iteration, ensure numerical stability with tolerance values

tried_paradigms.description: Replace the constraint-based optimization with a Voronoi-based geometric approach. Use scipy.spatial.Voronoi to compute the Voronoi diagram of circle centers, then set each circle's radius proportional to its distance to the nearest Voronoi vertex (representing available space). This creates a feedback loop where radii are determined by geometry rather than optimization constraints. The algorithm iterates: (1) compute Voronoi diagram, (2) set radii based on Voronoi cell size, (3) adjust positions to equalize radii or maximize sum, (4) repeat until convergence. This fundamentally differs from the constraint-based approach by using Voronoi geometry to naturally determine optimal spacing rather than enforcing constraints through optimization.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Primary sum_radii metric by leveraging natural geometric relationships between circle positions and available space through Voronoi tessellation
tried_paradigms.cautions: Handle Voronoi points at infinity (boundary circles), ensure convergence with damping factors, may need regularization to prevent radii from becoming too large near boundaries

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.spatial.cKDTree for sequential greedy placement with spatial indexing
tried_paradigms.description: Implement a sequential greedy placement algorithm enhanced with spatial indexing. Use scipy.spatial.cKDTree to efficiently query available space when placing each circle. The algorithm places circles sequentially: (1) initialize empty KDTree, (2) for each circle, query the KDTree to find the location with maximum available space (furthest from existing circles), (3) compute optimal radius at that location, (4) add to KDTree. After initial placement, optionally apply a local refinement using gradient-based adjustment on circle positions. This approach differs fundamentally from optimization-based methods by building the solution incrementally rather than adjusting all circles simultaneously, which can avoid local optima that trap gradient methods.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Primary sum_radii metric by using greedy placement that maximizes each circle's contribution sequentially, potentially finding better global configurations than simultaneous optimization
tried_paradigms.cautions: Greedy approach may be sensitive to placement order, consider multiple orderings or randomized restarts, ensure KDTree queries are efficient with appropriate leafsize parameter

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.spatial.Voronoi for iterative radius expansion based on cell boundaries
tried_paradigms.description: Instead of using Voronoi just for refinement, use it as the core optimization engine. Compute Voronoi diagram of circle centers, then for each circle calculate the minimum distance to its Voronoi cell boundary (which represents the closest constraint from neighbors or square edges). Set each radius to this distance, then adjust centers to maximize the sum of these Voronoi-limited radii. Iterate this process: recompute Voronoi, update radii, move centers toward local Voronoi cell centers, repeat until convergence. This directly exploits the geometric structure of circle packing where each circle's maximum radius is determined by its nearest constraints.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Use Voronoi cell geometry to find the optimal balance between circle positions and their maximum possible radii, directly maximizing sum of radii through geometric constraints
tried_paradigms.cautions: Voronoi diagram may have infinite cells for boundary circles - need to clip to unit square. Handle numerical precision carefully when computing distances to Voronoi vertices. May need to add small buffer to avoid exact touching that causes instability.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.integrate.solve_ivp for force-directed simulation with physical dynamics
tried_paradigms.description: Model circles as physical objects with repulsion forces. For each pair of circles, apply a force proportional to the overlap (if any) or inverse distance squared (for non-overlapping). Add boundary forces pushing circles away from square edges when close. Use scipy.integrate.solve_ivp to simulate the dynamics over time, allowing circles to 'settle' into a stable configuration. The key insight is that physical simulation naturally handles the complex constraint interactions without explicit constraint formulation. Use velocity damping to ensure convergence to a stable state. This is fundamentally different from gradient-based optimization as it uses continuous-time dynamics.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Simulate physical forces to naturally resolve overlaps and boundary violations while expanding radii, letting the system self-organize into a high-density packing
tried_paradigms.cautions: Need to carefully tune force magnitudes and damping to avoid oscillation or getting stuck. Must ensure simulation runs long enough to converge but within timeout. Force scaling is critical - too strong causes instability, too weak causes slow convergence.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.spatial.distance.cdist for greedy sequential placement with size ordering
tried_paradigms.description: Instead of placing circles randomly or in a hexagonal pattern, use a greedy algorithm that places circles in order of expected size. First place the largest possible circle at center. Then iteratively place remaining circles at positions that maximize their radius given existing circles, using scipy.spatial.distance.cdist to efficiently compute distances to all existing circles. After initial placement, use a local improvement phase: try swapping circle positions or adjusting radii in batches. The key is that cdist enables efficient computation of all pairwise distances, making greedy placement with lookahead feasible. Order circles by expected size (larger first) to maximize total sum.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Greedy placement strategy with distance-based selection to place larger circles first in optimal positions, then fill remaining space with smaller circles
tried_paradigms.cautions: Greedy can get stuck in local optima - need multiple restarts with different ordering strategies. cdist is efficient but still O(n^2) so keep iteration counts reasonable. Need to handle the sequential nature carefully to avoid early poor decisions.
